cues.text: Statistics summarizes a collection of observations without preserving every
individual detail in each summary.
The arithmetic mean is the sum of all observations divided by their positive
count.
The median is the middle observation after sorting, or the mean of the two
central observations when the count is even.
The mode is a value of greatest frequency.
For the sorted data one, two, two, five, the mean is ten divided by four, or
five halves.
The two central observations are both two, so the median is two, and the
unique
mode is also two.
These summaries need not coincide in general.
A data set may have several tied modes, or no single most frequent value.
Do not use the middle of an unsorted list as its median.
Repeated observations count separately when computing the mean and the
position
of the median.
An extreme observation can move the mean substantially while leaving the
median
unchanged.
State which measure is requested and retain the original data units in a
numerical answer.
A summary is not a substitute for checking how many observations each value
represents.
A frequency table records how many times each value occurs.
Its total count N is the sum of the frequencies, not the number of displayed
rows.
Multiply each value by its frequency, add those products and divide by N to
obtain the mean.
Values one, two and three with frequencies one, two and one have total count
four and weighted sum eight, giving mean two.
Taking the unweighted mean of table rows is generally wrong unless their
frequencies are equal.
A grouped continuous table instead gives intervals, so the exact individual
observations are unavailable.
Use each class mark, the midpoint of its two boundaries, as a representative
value when estimating the grouped mean.
For interval ten through twenty, the class mark is fifteen.
Classes zero to ten, ten to twenty and twenty to thirty with frequencies two,
five and three have estimated mean sixteen.
This is a grouped estimate, not a claim that every original observation equals
its midpoint.
Use consistent continuous boundaries and nonnegative frequencies, with a
positive total.
An empty class contributes zero to the weighted sum but may still matter when
reading neighbouring classes in a modal calculation.
For a grouped continuous distribution, the median formula interpolates inside
the class where cumulative frequency first reaches the halfway count.
Let L be its lower boundary and h its width.
Call the class frequency lower case f, and call the cumulative frequency
before
the class capital F.
First calculate N over two minus capital F, then divide by lower case f,
multiply by h and add L.
For classes zero to ten, ten to twenty and twenty to thirty with frequencies
two, five and three, N is ten.
The median class is ten to twenty, and the estimate is ten plus three fifths
of
ten, or sixteen.
For equal width classes with a single modal peak, the mode estimate uses modal
frequency f one and the neighbouring frequencies f zero and f two.
It is L plus f one minus f zero, divided by twice f one minus f zero minus f
two, times h.
The same table gives sixteen.
These are interpolation estimates from grouped data; they do not recover
unique
exact raw medians or modes.
Use boundaries rather than inconsistent printed limits, check the required
denominators and inspect ties or edge classes before applying a modal formula
blindly.
Mean deviation about a specified centre is the average of the absolute
deviations from that centre.
The absolute values are essential: signed deviations from the arithmetic mean
cancel, which would incorrectly suggest no spread.
For one, two, three, four, five, the mean is three and the absolute deviations
are two, one, zero, one and two.
Their average is six fifths.
The centre must be named because mean deviation about the mean can differ from
mean deviation about the median.
For one, two and nine, the median is two, so mean deviation about it is one
plus zero plus seven divided by three, or eight thirds.
The mean is four and mean deviation about that mean is ten thirds.
A median minimizes the sum of absolute distances, although the minimizing
centre need not be unique for an even count.
Frequency tables weight each absolute deviation by its frequency.
Grouped tables use class marks, producing an estimate of the corresponding raw
data spread.
Mean deviation has the same units as the observations and is always
nonnegative.
Check that a zero result means all represented observations equal the chosen
centre.
Variance measures spread through squared deviations from the arithmetic mean.
For the descriptive distribution formulas in this class, add the squared
deviations and divide by the total number N of observations.
Standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of that variance.
For data two, four and six, the mean is four.
Squared deviations are four, zero and four, giving variance eight thirds and
standard deviation square root of eight thirds.
Do not confuse standard deviation with variance or mean deviation: they use
different operations.
Variance has squared data units, while standard deviation has the same units
as
the observations.
Both are nonnegative, and zero variance means every observation is equal to
the mean.
Some statistical inference problems instead use divisor N minus one for an
unbiased sample variance estimator.
That is a different specified convention; do not substitute it into the
descriptive JEE distribution calculations here.
Always identify which definition the problem requests.
Carry exact fractions through the variance calculation before rounding the
square root, since premature rounding can distort comparisons or produce an
apparent negative result from a shortcut formula.
Expanding the squared deviation formula gives a useful shortcut: variance
equals the weighted mean of the squared values minus the square of the
weighted
mean.
For values one, two and three with frequencies one, two and one, N is four,
the
mean is two and the weighted second moment is eighteen divided by four, or
nine
halves.
The variance is therefore one half.
Squaring the weighted mean is different from averaging squared values, so keep
both parts visible.
For grouped classes with marks five, fifteen and twenty five and frequencies
two, five and three, the estimated mean is sixteen.
The weighted second moment is three hundred and five, giving variance three
hundred and five minus two hundred and fifty six, or forty nine, and standard
deviation seven.
These grouped results are based on representing observations by their class
marks.
They are not exact raw data variances without further within class
information.
Directly summing weighted squared deviations provides an independent check on
the shortcut.
Use nonnegative frequencies, a positive total and enough numerical precision
to
avoid cancellation errors when the mean is large relative to the spread.
An affine transformation changes every observation by the same rule Y equal to
a X plus b.
The new mean is a times the old mean plus b.
Subtracting that new mean from each transformed value leaves a times the
original deviation, so variance is multiplied by a squared.
Standard deviation is multiplied by absolute a, and mean deviation about the
correspondingly transformed centre is also multiplied by absolute a.
Adding a constant alone changes location but not spread.
For X values two, four and six, the mean is four and variance is eight thirds.
Transforming by negative two X plus five gives one, negative three and
negative
seven.
Their mean is negative three, variance is thirty two thirds and standard
deviation is twice square root of eight thirds.
The negative multiplier reverses ordering but cannot make a spread negative.
If a is zero, every transformed observation equals b and the dispersion is
zero.
A direct calculation on the transformed data checks the formulas.
Apply the transformation to each original observation or class mark
consistently; transforming frequencies themselves is not the same operation.
Probability starts with a random experiment and a sample space containing its
possible elementary outcomes.
An event is a subset of that sample space.
For two fair independent coin tosses recorded in order, the sample space is H
H, H T, T H and T T.
Each has probability one quarter.
Exactly one head corresponds to H T and T H, so its probability is one half.
Writing only zero heads, one head and two heads as equally likely outcomes
would be wrong, because the middle count represents two elementary outcomes.
A favourable count divided by a total count is valid for a finite sample space
only when those counted outcomes are equally likely.
Fairness, independence, replacement and whether order is recorded are
modelling
assumptions that must be stated.
If outcomes have unequal probabilities, add their assigned probability weights
instead of using an unweighted ratio.
Two physically different outcomes can produce the same later numerical
statistic without becoming one equally likely elementary outcome.
Before using a counting formula, identify exactly what is being counted and
whether each counted object has the same chance under the experiment.
A probability assigns a nonnegative weight to events, with total probability
of
the sample space equal to one.
Disjoint event probabilities add, and these facts imply every event
probability
lies between zero and one.
The impossible event, the empty set, has probability zero.
The complement of A contains all outcomes in the sample space that are not in
A.
Since A and its complement are disjoint and together exhaustive, their
probabilities add to one.
If P of A is three tenths, its complement has probability seven tenths.
The complement is relative to the chosen sample space, so that space must
remain fixed while using the formula.
At least one success is often easier to calculate as one minus the probability
of no successes, provided the no success event has been modelled correctly.
A probability of zero need not imply logical impossibility in every infinite
model, although the finite positive equally likely examples here have that
simpler interpretation.
Do not use a negative probability to compensate for a counting mistake.
Check the final range and whether the event and its complement together cover
the whole experiment.
The addition law calculates the probability that A or B or both occurs.
Adding P of A and P of B counts their intersection twice, so subtract its
probability once.
On a fair die, let A be the even outcomes two, four and six, and B be outcomes
greater than three, namely four, five and six.
Each event has probability one half.
Their intersection is four and six with probability one third.
Their union contains two, four, five and six, giving probability two thirds,
also one half plus one half minus one third.
Mutually exclusive events have empty intersection, so their probabilities add
directly.
Exclusivity is a condition to check, not an assumption attached to the word
or.
The probability of exactly one of A and B equals their union probability minus
their intersection probability.
In this die example it is one third.
A set list or Venn diagram helps verify the overlap and whether
the event wording includes both.
For three events, additional intersection corrections are needed; applying the
two event formula repeatedly is valid when each intermediate event and overlap
is handled consistently.
Conditional probability restricts attention to outcomes in an event already
known to occur.
P of B given A is the probability of their intersection divided by P of A,
provided that denominator is positive.
Rearranging gives the multiplication law P of A and B equal to P of A times P
of B given A.
A bag contains three red balls and two blue balls.
Draw twice uniformly without replacement.
The first red probability is three fifths.
After a red first draw, two red balls remain among four balls, so the
conditional probability of another red is one half.
Multiplication gives probability three tenths for two reds.
With replacement and a fresh uniform draw, the second red probability remains
three fifths and both red has probability nine twenty fifths.
These are different experiments.
Do not replace a conditional factor by an unconditional one unless
independence
has been established.
Conditioning on an event of probability zero is not defined by this elementary
ratio formula.
The order of the conditioning statement matters: P of B given A and P of A
given B are generally different quantities.
Events are independent when their intersection probability equals the product
of their separate probabilities.
If the conditioning event has positive probability, this also means learning
that event does not change the probability of the other.
For two fair independent tosses, A being a head on the first and B being a
head
on the second each has probability one half, while their intersection H H has
probability one quarter.
Thus these events are independent and can occur together.
Mutually exclusive events instead cannot occur together.
If both have positive probability, their intersection probability zero differs
from the positive product, so they are not independent.
A zero probability event is a degenerate exception in the algebraic
independence test.
Replacement can help produce independent draws in a specified model, but
independence should not be inferred solely from a visual separation of two
events or from the fact that they have equal probabilities.
For three or more events, pairwise independence does not automatically imply
mutual independence.
In any multiplication calculation, identify which independence assumption is
being used and check it against the experiment rather than substituting a
product by habit.
The law of total probability breaks an event into mutually exclusive source
paths.
Suppose the source events form a partition of the sample space: exactly one
occurs and together they include all outcomes.
Then multiply each source probability by the conditional target probability in
that source and add the contributions.
Choose box one with probability two fifths and box two with probability three
fifths.
A uniform ball drawn from box one is red with probability three quarters, and
one from box two is red with probability one quarter.
The overall red probability is two fifths times three quarters plus three
fifths times one quarter.
The contributions are three tenths and three twentieths, totalling nine
twentieths.
An unweighted average of three quarters and one quarter would incorrectly
assume equal box selection probabilities.
A probability tree makes the source weights and target likelihoods explicit.
At each branching stage the alternatives must match the actual experiment.
Total probability is an addition over disjoint paths, while each path
probability uses the multiplication law.
Check that all relevant sources are included once, and that no overlapping
source event is counted twice.
Bayes theorem reverses a conditional question by combining a source's prior
weight with its likelihood of the observed event and dividing by the total
probability of that event.
In the preceding box model, the probability of selecting box one and then
drawing red is three tenths.
The total probability of red from either box is nine twentieths.
Given that the drawn ball is red, the probability that box one was selected is
three tenths divided by nine twentieths, or two thirds.
This posterior differs from the original box one selection probability two
fifths.
The observation favours the box in which red is more likely, but the prior
weights still matter.
Do not simply reverse P of red given box one, which was three quarters.
The denominator must include all disjoint exhaustive source paths and must be
positive.
The corresponding posterior for box two is one third, so the posterior source
probabilities sum to one.
A tree or contingency table can verify the same ratios.
State precisely what information has been observed before deciding which
probability is the conditioning denominator.
A random variable assigns a real number to each outcome of a random
experiment.
It is a function of the outcome, rather than a new equally likely elementary
outcome list.
Let X be the number of heads in two fair independent tosses.
T T maps to zero, H T and T H map to one, and H H maps to two.
The probability distribution therefore gives probabilities one quarter, one
half and one quarter to values zero, one and two.
The middle value has greater probability because two elementary outcomes
produce it.
A discrete probability mass function must assign nonnegative probabilities
whose total over all possible values is one.
Use these two conditions to determine or reject an unknown probability
parameter.
A table with correct total but a negative entry is still invalid.
For an event such as X at least one, add the masses at one and two, obtaining
three quarters.
A distribution summarizes the numerical random variable without making H T and
T H the same underlying outcome.
Check that every possible value is included and that a listed value is paired
with its own probability rather than with a frequency from an unrelated
sample.
The expectation of a finite discrete random variable is the probability
weighted sum of its values.
For the head count distribution zero, one and two with probabilities one
quarter, one half and one quarter, the expectation is one.
The second moment E of X squared is zero plus one half plus four quarters, or
three halves.
Variance equals this second moment minus the square of the expectation, giving
one half.
Equivalently, directly average the squared deviations from the expectation
using the probability weights.
Standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of that variance.
Expectation need not be a value the random variable can actually take in every
example; it is a weighted average, not a guaranteed future outcome.
A constant random variable has zero variance.
For Y equal to a X plus b, expectation changes to a E of X plus b
and variance to a squared times the original variance, matching the
descriptive
data transformation rules.
Keep E of X squared distinct from the square of E of X, and check nonnegative
variance and total probability one before interpreting the numerical results.
